passages.t: The place the LORD will choose
passages.happening:
The detailed laws begin. “These are the statutes and ordinances you must be careful to follow all the days you live in the land” (verse 1).

The first is about worship. Israel is to destroy the places where the nations of the land served their gods, ‘atop the high mountains, on the hills, and under every green tree’ (verse 2). Their altars, pillars and poles are to come down (verse 3). “You shall not worship the LORD your God in this way” (verse 4).

“Instead, you must seek the place the LORD your God will choose from among all your tribes to establish as a dwelling for His Name, and there you must go” (verse 5). Offerings, tithes and gifts are to be brought there (verse 6). “There, in the presence of the LORD your God, you and your households shall eat and rejoice in all you do” (verse 7).

Things are looser now, in the wilderness, ‘where everyone does what seems right in his own eyes’ (verse 8). When Israel has rest in the land, God will choose the place (verses 10-11). “And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God”, with sons and daughters, servants, and the Levite who has no land of his own (verse 12). Burnt offerings are not to be made ‘in just any place you see’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 12 to 26 are the laws for life in the land. It is worth noticing what comes first. The first law is not about property or crime. It is about worship.

The religion of Canaan was local. Shrines stood on hilltops, which were thought to be nearer the gods, and under leafy trees, which were linked with fertility. Each town could have its own altar, its own standing stones and its own form of the god.

Moses commands the opposite. There will be one sanctuary for the whole nation, and God will choose it. The people will not. This kept Israel from mixing its God with the gods of each hill, and from making worship into whatever each clan thought best. That is the meaning of verse 8.

The key phrase is ‘the place the LORD your God will choose’. The Hebrew word for ‘place’ comes nine times in the chapter. The place is never named in the book. Leaving it unnamed keeps the weight on God's choice and not on the fame of any city.

God will make his Name ‘dwell’ there. The Hebrew verb is the root of the word for the tabernacle. The phrase says that God is truly present at the place. It does not say that he is shut inside a building.

And worship there is a feast. The offerings are eaten by the family together, with the servants and the Levites. Three times this chapter commands joy. In Deuteronomy gladness before God is part of obedience.

The list of who is to rejoice reaches down the household to the people most easily left out: daughters as well as sons, female servants as well as male, and the Levite who owns no field.

The command to destroy the shrines of the land belongs with chapter 7. The note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, sets out how Christians read those commands. It is a command to ancient Israel about the worship sites of Canaan. No one may use it as a reason to damage any place of worship or to harm any person.
passages.later:
Jeremiah names an earlier place than Jerusalem. God says through him, ‘go now to the place in Shiloh where I first made a dwelling for My Name’ (Jeremiah 7:12).

When Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem he prayed with this chapter's words: ‘toward the place of which You said, “My Name shall be there”’ (1 Kings 8:29).

The book of Judges uses the words of verse 8 for the disorder of a later time: “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25).

John's Gospel says of Jesus, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). Jesus spoke of ‘the temple of His body’ (John 2:21). And he told a Samaritan woman that a time was coming ‘when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth’ (John 4:23).
passages.hard:
When was this law given, and which place is meant?

The chapter stands at the center of the debate about when Deuteronomy was written.

Many scholars since the nineteenth century have linked it with the reforms of two kings of Judah. King Hezekiah ‘removed the high places’ (2 Kings 18:4). King Josiah, about 622 BC, closed the shrines across the land and brought all worship to Jerusalem (2 Kings 23). On this view the law of the one place was written, or given its final shape, to support that reform.

Others hold that the principle is older. They point out that the chapter never names Jerusalem. It could have applied first to Shiloh, or to wherever the ark was kept. And Israel's earlier history already shows a central sanctuary alongside other altars.

Digging has added evidence and has not settled the matter. At Arad, in the south, a small shrine of the kingdom of Judah was found, with an altar and standing stones. Some date it to the eighth century BC and connect its end with Hezekiah's reform. Its dating is debated.

These notes take no side. On either view the point of the law is the same. Israel is to worship its God in the way and at the place that he chooses.
passages.asks: Moses says that Israel must not worship ‘in just any place you see’, which is to say, however seems best to each person. Ask how much of your worship is shaped by what God has said and how much by what suits you. And notice that the command is to rejoice, and to bring others into it. Ask who is at your table when you give thanks.

passages.t: Meat at home, and the blood
passages.happening:
A practical question follows from the one place. If sacrifice can be offered only there, what of meat eaten at home?

Moses answers. “But whenever you want, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your gates” (verse 15). It may be eaten as a gazelle or deer is eaten, by those who are ceremonially clean and those who are not.

One rule stays. “But you must not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water” (verse 16). He says it again with the reason: “Only be sure not to eat the blood, because the blood is the life, and you must not eat the life with the meat” (verse 23).

The holy things are different. Tithes, firstborn animals and offerings promised in a vow must be taken to the place God chooses and eaten there with joy (verses 17-18, 26-27). And Israel must not neglect the Levites (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world nearly all meat was eaten in connection with a sacrifice. An animal was brought to a shrine, part was offered, and the rest was eaten.

Once worship was gathered in one place, a family living far away would rarely be able to eat meat. So this law allows ordinary slaughter at home. A sheep or an ox may be treated like a gazelle or a deer. Those were wild animals that were eaten and were never offered on the altar.

The law makes room for ordinary life. ‘Whenever you want’ comes three times. Moses says that the wish for meat is no sin. God's command about worship is not meant to take food from the table.

But the blood is kept back. The ban on eating blood goes back to God's word to Noah after the flood, and it is repeated in Leviticus. The reason given is that ‘the blood is the life’. Pouring out the blood marked the difference between using an animal for food and taking its life, which belongs to God alone. Each time a family killed an animal for dinner, it was reminded that a life had been taken and that life is God's.

Jewish practice built careful ways of killing and salting meat so that the blood is drained from it, and keeps them today.

Christians differ on whether the rule about blood still applies to them. The note on Leviticus 17 sets out the readings and takes no side. It also gives a caution that belongs here. This law is about eating and about sacrifice. It was not written about modern medicine, and these notes are not medical advice.
passages.later:
God had said to Noah, “But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4).

Leviticus gives the fullest reason: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar” (Leviticus 17:11).

The first council of the church asked Gentile believers to abstain ‘from blood’ among a few other things (Acts 15:29).
passages.asks: The law reminded Israel at every meal that a life had been given for it. Ask whether you eat with any thought of what your food cost, or of who gave it. And notice how God's law bends to make room for a family far from the sanctuary. Ask whether you think of God's commands as made for people's good.

passages.t: ‘How do these nations serve their gods?’
passages.happening:
Moses ends with a warning about curiosity. When the nations are gone and Israel lives in their land, ‘be careful not to be ensnared by their ways’ (verse 30). Israel must not ask, ‘How do these nations serve their gods? I will do likewise.’

“You must not worship the LORD your God in this way, because they practice for their gods every abomination which the LORD hates. They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods” (verse 31).

“See that you do everything I command you; do not add to it or subtract from it” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The danger named here is not that Israel will leave its God for another. It is that Israel will go on worshiping the LORD and borrow the methods of its neighbors to do it. Verse 31 says ‘in this way’, as verse 4 did. The chapter opens and closes with the same warning.

Moses forbids even the question.

He gives one example, the worst. Some peoples of that world burned their own children as offerings. The Old Testament condemns this again and again. It reports with horror that two kings of Judah, Ahaz and Manasseh, later did it themselves, and that a king of Moab sacrificed his son on the city wall during a siege.

This verse matters for how the hard chapters of this book are read. When Deuteronomy speaks of the wickedness of the nations of the land, this is the kind of thing it names. And it shows what Israel's God is like. He hates the killing of children. No one could ever please him by it.

A reader should not make this verse into contempt for any people. The same sentence was later spoken against Israel's own kings.

The last verse forbids adding to God's commands or taking from them. It echoes 4:2. Worship is the place where people most want to improve on what God has said, by adding what impresses and removing what costs.
passages.later:
The books of Kings record that the warning was not heeded. King Ahaz ‘even sacrificed his son in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations’ (2 Kings 16:3).

God said through Jeremiah of those who did this in Jerusalem that it was ‘something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind’ (Jeremiah 7:31).

The New Testament says where God now makes his home: “And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22).
passages.asks: Israel was tempted to keep its God and borrow its neighbors' ways. Ask what you have taken into your faith from the world around you because it works, without asking whether God wants it. And hear what verse 31 says of God. He hates the harming of children. Ask whether the way you speak about him would lead anyone to think otherwise.
